name: Mitigatti (Gatti)
description: Mitigatti (also known as Gatti) is a traditional Italian trick-taking game played with a Tarot deck (Tarocchi). Popular in the Piedmont and Liguria regions, it is a complex game involving 78 cards, including 21 trumps and the Joker-like 'Matto'. It features a unique 'Bargaining' phase where players can negotiate to end a hand early based on their card strength, and scoring is based on both captured tricks and specific card combinations (declarations).
deck: 78-card tarot deck; historically Italian-suited Tarocco Piemontese, but by the Nice 1930 source often played with French-suited tarot cards

history.origins: Dates back centuries to the evolution of Tarot games in Northern Italy. It is closely related to 'Tarocchini' and 'Minchiate'.
timeline: 1700s: Early forms of Gatti are played in Turin and Genoa.
1800s: Bidding and bargaining systems become more formalized.
1950s: Modern ruleset for 3 players becomes the standard for regional clubs.
Present: Still played in specialized Tarot circles in Northwest Italy.
history.cultural: A symbol of regional identity, often played in local 'Circoli' (clubs) alongside games like Scopa and Briscola.
history.evolution: The game's most distinct feature, the 'Bargaining' (andare a monte), reflects the high variance of Tarot hands where luck can occasionally lead to unplayable distributions.

setup.deck: 78-card Italian-suited tarot pack. The Nice source describes the older Piedmontese / Marseille-style structure while noting that local players had largely switched to French-suited tarot cards by the early twentieth century.
setup.dealing: Each player receives 25 cards. The remaining 3 cards (the Talon) go to the dealer.

rules.objective: Score the most points through tricks, declarations, and ending-bonuses.
rules.gameplay: Must follow suit. If you can't, you MUST trump. The 'Matto' (Fool) can be played at any time and cannot win a trick, but stays with the player who played it.
keyRules: Must follow suit; if void in led suit, must trump.
The Matto (Fool) may be played at any time and does not win the trick; it remains with the player who played it.
Scoring is based on captured tricks and declaration combinations (declarations).
Bargaining (andare a monte) allows players to negotiate to end a hand early based on card strength.

strategy.basic: Keep track of the 'Angel' (Trump 20) and 'World' (Trump 21). These are your safety cards to regain the lead. If you have the 'Bagatto' (Trump 1), try to save it for the very last trick, but don't get caught if someone leads a trump you can't beat.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Matto' Save: Use the 'Matto' to avoid using a high trump on a trick you know you can't win. Since you get to keep the Matto regardless of the winner, it's effectively a 'pass' card that preserves your hand strength.
strategy.advanced: Bargaining Aggression: If you have a mediocre hand but hold two Kings, try to demand a higher 'fold' price in the bargaining phase. If the others have great trumps, they might pay you to just start a new hand rather than risk their points against your declarations.
tips: Memorize the suit directions! In Tarot, a 1 of Diamonds is higher than a 10, but a 10 of Spades is higher than an Ace.
Watch the 'Cavalier' cards. They are often the tipping point in trick captures.
